newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: FOCUS-Dud telecom deal clouds Kazakh privatisation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Dud telecom deal clouds Kazakh privatisation.

text.p: Kazakhstan said on Monday a deal to sell Deutsche Telekom AG a 49 percent share in its telecoms monopoly had fallen through, casting a shadow over the former Soviet republic's plans to speed up privatisation.

"A telegram was sent to the German side (from the Kazakh government) in which the heads of Deutsche Telekom were notified that talks to conclude the contract were over," said Kazakh state news agency Khabar-Press, quoting Saribay Kalmurzayev, the powerful head of the State Property Committee.
A banker close to the deal said Deutsche Telekom had double-checked its figures and found the deal too costly.
"The (Kazakh) government were charging too much for the stake," he said, adding that poor management at the enterprise was also a concern for the company.

A framework agreement signed with the Kazakh government in May last year saw the German telecoms group agree to pay off NAK Kazakhtelekom's debts and increase the oil-rich republic's 2.1 million telephone lines to 4.5 million within 10 years.
Under the agreement, Deutsche Telekom had the right to manage Kazakhtelekom for up to 15 years.

But as 1996 drew to a close and with Deutsche Telekom apparently no closer to completing the deal, the company was told last month by the Kazakh government it had until the end of the year to complete the contract.
Kalmurzayev said late last year that Kazakhtelekom's rising debts and Deutsche Telekom's desire for a monopoly over present and future telecoms services had been the main sticking points.

Of the 825 million marks ($527 million) Deutsche Telekom agreed to pay for the share, 460 million marks were earmarked to pay off a 1992 loan made to Kazakhtelekom by German investment agency Kreditanstalt fuer Wiederaufbau.
The soured telecoms deal is a setback for the Kazakh government which has vowed fast-track privatisation of large state enterprises and utilities.
Debts, often hidden in opaque accounts, are the main worry for foreign investors eyeing the republic's large enterprises for privatisation in the next few months.
The government aims to create a collection of "blue-chip" companies to form the basis of a new securities market while raising cash to pay off a backlog of unpaid wages and pensions.
The privatisation of Kazakhtelekom was held up by Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin last month as an example of how it was not selling the country off cheap to foreign companies.
Khabar-Press said the republic would announce a new tender for troubled Kazakhtelekom shortly but probably for a smaller stake than that offered Deutsche Telekom.
"For the next tender, the government needs to clarify the legal issues, in particular anti-monopoly legislation," said a Kazakh economist who declined to be named. ($1=1.5653 Mark)
